To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the introduction of point of sale tobacco display bans in Victoria and Western Australia was influenced by a number of factors, including a range of stakeholders and the evidence that they communicated to support their advocacy for a policy change.

the evidence communicated by the ‘stakeholders’ in this study was used to advocate for a point-of-sale display ban, and that the evidence was communicated in a manner that was not consistent with the principles of evidence‐based policy making.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the way that evidence is communicated to influence public policy and the role of ‘stakeholders’ in this process.
how the evidence is used and communicated by the various ‘stakeholders’ in the policy process.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the introduction of point of sale tobacco display bans was a political process, where the evidence was used by stakeholders to advocate for their preferred policy outcome.
tobacco control advocates used evidence to support their policy arguments.
the evidence for the effectiveness of the policy was strong.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

we were able to show that the policy was introduced in a way that allowed the evidence base to be used to support the policy, but that the evidence base was not used in a way that would be expected in a ‘rational’ policy process.
the policy process was not a linear process and evidence did not play a central role in the introduction of the policy.

there is a need for a more nuanced approach to evidence in policy-making, one that acknowledges that evidence is constructed by different groups of stakeholders in different ways and for different reasons, and that evidence is not always used in the same way by different groups of people, even when they have similar policy goals.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the policy process is not as linear as the policy cycle would suggest and that the way evidence is communicated and used in the policy process can have a significant impact on the way that policy decisions are made.

evidence was used by a range of stakeholders in the policy field, and the way in which evidence was used and presented to the policy field was not always consistent with the scientific method or the way in which it was presented by scientists.
evidence was used to support policy decisions and to justify the introduction of the ban.
